newsitem.title: INDIA: India's sugar exports seen rising in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: India's sugar exports seen rising in 1996/97.

text.p: India's sugar exports, egged on by surging European demand, could rise substantially in 1996/97 (October-September), industry officials said on Thursday.
"Indian sugar has a good potential in the European markets," Shivajirao Patil, president of the National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories (NFCSF), told Reuters.
He said India could also explore East African markets.

India produced an all-time high of 16.4 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 and the new season started with stocks as high as 8.1 million tonnes, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said while inaugurating a meeting of the NFCSF on Thursday.
"We can export upto 1.5 million tonnes in the current sugar year if the Sugar Act is not repealed," Patil said.
India exported a little more than one million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 at $365-375 per tonne FOB.

Last week, India's lower house of parliament approved a bill to repeal the Sugar Act under which the Indian Sugar and General Industries Export-Import Corp (ISGIEC), an agency set up by private millers, has a monopoly on exports.
But the upper house stalled the bill, telling the government that the issue needed further study.
The bill is facing opposition from domestic millers who say the move to allow more players could lead to an export price war that could eventually dry up exports.
"Once the act is repealed, it will lead to severe undercutting and losses will mount," M. S. Marathe, managing director of NFCSF, told Reuters.
The proposal to end ISGIEC's monopoly over sugar exports could backfire on the sugar industry as production costs are higher than international prices, millers say.
They say the cost of production of sugar in India is higher than export prices because of government controls.
Sugar supplies and prices in India are controlled by the government.
Private mills supply 40 percent of the national output and cooperative mills account for the rest.
The mills are obliged to sell 40 percent of their output to the government at below market rates for distribution through government shops at subsidised prices.

The mills sell the balance in the open market, but their supplies are controlled by quotas announced every month by the government, which keeps a check on physical arrivals in the market to regulate price levels and control inflation.
Millers say it costs about 11,500-12,000 rupees to manufacture a tonne of sugar but the produce is supplied to the government at 8,800 rupees per tonne.
Patil said only a few "rich" sugar factories will be able to export sugar if the Sugar Act was repealed.
"The high level of production has created liquidity problems for the industry," Deve Gowda said.
The government had created a buffer stock of one million tonnes, encouraged export of sugar and released high quantities of sugar for sale in the market, Deve Gowda said.
